query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing about 1 wt% oxygen, a predictive framework that combines ab initio simulations with an active-learning machine‐learning component—which explicitly models microstructural defects (e.g., Ta clustering and oxygen‐induced defect states) and their effect on electron scattering—will yield electrical conductivity predictions that closely match experimental observations over both the cryogenic (0–200 K) regime and the high‐temperature (300–1200 K) regime. In particular, the model will predict a significantly lowered conductivity at low temperatures due to enhanced defect scattering, while at high temperatures the incorporation of phonon scattering effects plus defect corrections will narrow the error margin relative to conventional models that assume perfect crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy with realistic microstructural inhomogeneities (such as one-dimensional Ta clusters) and approximately 1 wt% oxygen impurity.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply an active-learning enhanced ab initio framework that incorporates explicit defect configurations (including oxygen-induced defects) into conductivity calculations via machine-learned interatomic potentials and extended sampling of defective configurations.
generation.conditions: The predictive model will be applied over two temperature regimes: 0–200 K, where defect-induced electron scattering dominates, and 300–1200 K, where phonon scattering plays a larger role. The study is specific to bulk specimens of HfNbTaTiZr with ~1 wt% oxygen contamination.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical inhomogeneities arising from Ta clustering (as seen in Monte Carlo simulations) and oxygen-induced defects (including possible oxide precursor formation and defect-states) that modify electron relaxation times.
generation.mechanism: By explicitly including microstructural defects and oxygen impurity effects in the simulation, the model adjusts the effective plasma frequency and electron relaxation time. This modification accounts for additional scattering events that are absent in perfect-crystal analytical predictions, thereby reducing the overestimation of conductivity observed when using ideal solution (‘cocktail effect’) models.
generation.predicted_outcome: The improved predictive model will forecast an electrical conductivity that drops significantly (for example, by over 30% relative to ideal-crystal estimates) in the cryogenic regime due to enhanced defect scattering, while at higher temperatures (300–1200 K) the predictions will lie within approximately 15–20% of experimental values. Overall, the model is expected to reduce the prediction error (relative to conventional analytical approaches) by nearly 50% across the studied temperature range.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical predictions assume a perfect, defect-free crystal and typically yield conductivity estimates that may be off by an order of magnitude, especially in the cryogenic regime.
generation.boundary: This approach is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloys with oxygen contamination up to about 1 wt%. Its accuracy is expected to be reliable between 0 K and 1200 K, beyond which additional high-temperature effects may need further modeling.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contribution of defect scattering—especially at 0–200 K—is extrapolated by combining insights from ab initio Monte Carlo microstructure simulations (PMC7514597) and oxygen contamination studies (PMC6926650) with the novel ML-enhanced framework (PMC11275555). The precise magnitude of conductivity reduction in the cryogenic regime is estimated and remains uncertain until validated by experiment.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with a confirmed oxygen content around 1 wt% and characterize their microstructure to confirm the presence of defect features (e.g., Ta clustering). Measure the electrical conductivity at multiple temperatures spanning the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes. Compare these empirical conductivity values with the predictions from the new ML-enhanced model and with conventional analytical predictions that assume a perfect crystal.
measurements: Electrical conductivity values at selected temperatures (e.g., 50 K, 150 K, 300 K, 600 K, 900 K, 1200 K)
Structural characterization using TEM/SEM/EDX to verify defect distributions and oxygen incorporation
Oxygen concentration verification by inert gas fusion or similar methods
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-enhanced defect-inclusive model does not reduce the prediction error by at least 50% compared to conventional analytical models (e.g., if the measured conductivity at any temperature deviates by an order-of-magnitude from the model predictions or the error margins remain statistically indistinguishable from those of defect-free assumptions), then the hypothesis is falsified.

While first-principles methods have been successfully applied to characterize individual properties of multi-principal element alloys (MPEA), their use in searching for optimal trade-offs between competing properties is hampered by high computational demands. In this work, we present a framework to explore Pareto-optimal compositions by integrating advanced ab initio-based techniques into a Bayesian multi-objective optimization workflow, complemented by a simple analytical model providing straightforward analysis of trends. HfNbTaTiZr high entropy alloy was produced by various methods of powder metallurgy including mechanical alloying, sintering, hot isostatic pressing, spark plasma sintering, and high pressure torsion. The microstructure and mechanical properties of HfNbTaTiZr prepared by various methods were examined. It was found that the main problem in fabrication of HfNbTaTiZr alloy by powder metallurgy is oxygen contamination. Samples prepared by cold isostatic pressing followed by sintering and/or hot isostatic pressing contained oxygen in the concentration range of 0.55 wt %–0.85 wt %. Oxygen contamination of samples prepared by mechanical alloying was even higher, and the oxygen concentration in these samples exceeded 1 wt %. Oxygen incorporated into the HfNbTaTiZr samples caused deterioration of mechanical properties (embrittlement) and prevented formation of a single phase random solid solution. Investigations performed in the present work showed that the most promising powder metallurgy method of production of HfNbTaTiZr alloy was spark plasma sintering of gas atomized powder. cited_evidence.text: Ab-initio MC simulation was performed to evaluate the microstructure stability of investigated alloys. Simulation was performed for the 5 element HfNbTaTiZr alloy, because it contains all elements considered in investigated alloys. Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, Zr ions were distributed randomly in equimolar concentration into a 250 atom BCC supercell. This initial state was relaxed with respect to ion positions until minimum of the total free energy was reached. The equilibrium configuration corresponding to minimum free energy was obtained using a Metropolis MC algorithm at 300 K (room temperature). The details of the simulation and more complete results will be published elsewhere. Figure 7 shows the equilibrium atomic configuration corresponding to the minimum of total energy. The most apparent effect is a rather one-dimensional Ta object (‘wire’) along the <100> direction. The Ta wire is surrounded predominantly by Nb ions. The rest of the simulation box is filled up by the mixture of Ti, Zr and Hf. The latter two elements appear to be well separated from the Ta and Nb region.
